slides.title: Doors only staff may open
slides.text: At the post office, some doors only staff may open. That rule decides who can get to the letters inside, and who must stay out.

slides.title: Your tablet does it too
slides.text: A tablet lock screen does the same job at home. Only a person with permission, and the right key or code, can open it and see inside.
slides.alt: A tablet holds messages and pictures. Signing out on a shared computer: does the habit protect it, or is it risky?

focus.cue: A tablet holds your messages and pictures: sort what protects it

slides.title: A found key is not enough
slides.text: Mina loses her mailbox key, and a stranger finds it. A second lock still keeps her mailbox shut, because the stranger is missing one more thing.
steps: a second lock asks for a code
a code arrives on a phone at home

slides.title: A spare copy, kept elsewhere
slides.text: A backup is a spare copy of your things, kept somewhere else, like photos saved in another place. Your passphrase is different: it stays in your head, never in a copy.
slides.alt: Lock It, the spare-copy sort: a copy in the family’s online folder. A good spare copy, or not a spare copy?

focus.cue: A copy in the family's online folder: a spare kept elsewhere

slides.title: The wrong person
slides.text: Finding a tablet on a bench does not make it yours to open. A letter that asks for your mailbox key is the wrong person too: only you and a trusted adult may know it.
slides.alt: A game chat from Someone at the Park with both clues marked: “I found a tablet on the bench with your sticker on it!” and “Tell me its unlock code”.

focus.cue: Finding a tablet does not make it theirs to open

slides.text: Open Trick Inbox at Key Keepers and sort all 6 messages. Tap every clue, then choose a move. Friends, fixers and finders ask for your key, but only you and a trusted adult may know it.
